scenes.text: Put 100 units of electricity in. Get about 28 back. That's what engineers at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory in Colorado, now the National Laboratory of the Rockies, reported in 2024 after a megawatt-scale test: electricity into hydrogen, into storage, and back into electricity.
That was one research test system, running at full power. At low power, about 35 came back.
scenes.graphic: bar chart: electricity returned per 100 units stored. Hydrogen system, NREL ARIES test (2024): 28.3 at full power, 35.1 at low power. U.S. utility-scale battery fleet (EIA, 2019): 82

scenes.text: Now compare that with a whole fleet of batteries. In 2019, the EIA found that America's grid batteries gave back about 82 percent. That's called round-trip efficiency.
So why did the federal government commit billions of dollars to hydrogen? And why might the hydrogen that matters most already be on your dinner table?
Both answers come down to one idea: hydrogen isn't really a fuel problem, it's a where-do-you-use-it problem. So let's follow the electron, and see where turning it into a molecule is worth the trip.

First, what hydrogen actually is. It's the most abundant element in the universe, but on Earth it comes combined with other elements: with oxygen in water, or with carbon in natural gas, coal and oil.
So before we can use it, we have to pull it apart. The EIA calls hydrogen an energy carrier: it moves energy from one place to another, a bit like electricity.
And carrying has a price. In the EIA's words, producing hydrogen requires more energy than hydrogen provides when it's converted to useful energy.
America already makes plenty of it: about 10 million metric tons a year, according to the Energy Department's 2023 hydrogen strategy.
The Energy Department says about 95 percent of U.S. hydrogen is made from natural gas, in large plants that use a process called steam-methane reforming.
scenes.graphic: donut chart: U.S. hydrogen production, about 10 million metric tons per year (DOE); 95% from natural gas reforming, 5% other routes

scenes.text: Methane and steam meet at 1,300 to 1,800 degrees Fahrenheit. Out come hydrogen and carbon monoxide, and a second step turns that carbon monoxide into carbon dioxide and more hydrogen.
scenes.graphic: diagram: steam-methane reforming. Step 1: CH4 + H2O (+ heat) -> CO + 3 H2. Step 2 (water-gas shift): CO + H2O -> CO2 + H2. Then CO2 and impurities removed (DOE)

scenes.text: That carbon dioxide adds up. The Energy Department's 2023 hydrogen strategy put U.S. hydrogen production at about 100 million metric tons of greenhouse gases a year.
Capture most of that carbon and store it underground, and people often call the result blue hydrogen. Let it go into the air, and it's called grey.
The other main route is electrolysis: running an electric current through water to split it into hydrogen and oxygen. With wind or solar power, that's usually called green hydrogen.
Either way, the IEA says low-emission hydrogen was still less than 1 percent of global production in 2024.
Here's where the electron comes in. The Energy Department's 2022 status figure for a typical electrolyzer system was about 55 kilowatt-hours of electricity for every kilogram of hydrogen.
scenes.graphic: bar chart: electrolyzer system electricity use, kWh per kg hydrogen (share of energy kept, LHV): 2022 status 55 (61%), 2026 target 51 (65%), ultimate target 46 (72%) (DOE PEM targets)

scenes.text: Only about 61 percent of that electricity's energy ends up stored in the hydrogen. The department's long-term targets are around 70 percent.

Then the hydrogen has to be stored. It holds more energy per pound than any other fuel, but very little per gallon, so it gets squeezed into tanks at up to 10,000 psi or chilled into a liquid at minus 423 degrees Fahrenheit.

Now stack the losses. That's the chain from the start of this video: electricity to hydrogen, then back to electricity. In that Colorado test, the fuel cell generator alone turned only about half of the hydrogen's energy back into electricity.
A hydrogen car runs the same chain. Its fuel cell turns hydrogen back into electricity for an electric motor. A battery car skips the detour and stores the electricity directly.

Now look at the fueling map. As of November 2026, the Energy Department's station locator lists 44 hydrogen fueling stations in the whole country, 42 of them in California. It lists nearly 84,000 charging locations for electric cars.
scenes.graphic: bar chart (log scale or icon grid): U.S. alternative fueling station counts, AFDC, data as of Nov 7, 2026: hydrogen 44 stations (38 retail, 6 non-retail; 42 in California) vs. electric vehicle charging 83,972 station locations (excludes residential chargers)

scenes.text: Home heating has the same problem, only sharper. The Energy Department says a heat pump can deliver up to three times more heat than the energy it uses.
Turn that same electricity into hydrogen, and nearly 40 percent of the energy is gone before you light a burner. And hydrogen packs only about a third of natural gas's energy by volume.
scenes.graphic: two-path diagram from 1 unit of electricity: heat pump -> up to 3 units of heat (DOE); electrolysis -> about 0.61 units of energy in hydrogen (DOE 2022 status), before any burner losses

scenes.text: So for cars and homes, where electricity can do the job directly, hydrogen is the long way around.
But flip the question. What if you don't need energy, but the hydrogen atoms themselves? That's where it makes sense, not as a fuel, but as an ingredient.
Oil refineries are one. They use hydrogen to remove sulfur from fuels. Worldwide, refining used more than 43 million metric tons of hydrogen in 2024.
scenes.graphic: bar chart: global hydrogen demand 2024 (IEA): oil refining >43 Mt; industry 55 Mt, of which ammonia 60%, methanol 30%, steel (DRI) 10%; new applications <1% of total

scenes.text: Fertilizer is the big one. Hydrogen plus nitrogen from the air makes ammonia, and in the U.S., 88 percent of ammonia goes into fertilizer. So in a sense, that's the hydrogen on your dinner table.
Worldwide, ammonia takes about 60 percent of the hydrogen used in industry. Switch to clean hydrogen, and the Energy Department says ammonia plants could cut their emissions by more than 90 percent.
Steel is next. About 70 percent of American steel is made by melting mostly scrap in electric furnaces. But making new steel from iron ore relies on coke and natural gas.
Use clean hydrogen to pull the oxygen out of the ore instead, and the Energy Department says the life-cycle emissions of new steel could drop by 40 to 70 percent.
Then come the maybes. Ships could run on fuels made from hydrogen, like ammonia and methanol.
Heavy trucks are another maybe. The Energy Department says fuel cells suit trucks that need diesel-like fill times or ranges above 500 miles.

And the grid could store hydrogen for days or even weeks, the EIA says, while the average U.S. grid battery in 2019 held about an hour and a half of output. In Utah, a project backed by a federal loan guarantee is designed to pair a 220-megawatt electrolyzer with salt caverns.

Which brings us back to the billions. The 2021 infrastructure law gave the Energy Department 9.5 billion dollars for hydrogen. In 2023, the Energy Department selected seven regional hydrogen hubs, with 7 billion dollars in funding.
Its national strategy aims for 10 million metric tons of clean hydrogen a year by 2030, 20 million by 2040, and 50 million by 2050.
scenes.graphic: column chart: DOE National Clean Hydrogen Strategy (2023) goals for clean hydrogen: 10 MMT/yr (2030), 20 (2040), 50 (2050); reference line: today's total U.S. production about 10 MMT/yr, 95% from natural gas

scenes.text: But plans have met reality. In October 2025, the Energy Department cancelled funding for the California and Pacific Northwest hubs. In April 2026, it said it would keep nearly 5 billion dollars for the other five.
Quick recap. Hydrogen is a carrier, not a source. America makes most of it from natural gas, and turning electricity into hydrogen and back loses most of the energy.
That's why it struggles in cars and homes, where electricity works directly. But in refineries, fertilizer and steel, the molecule itself is the point.
Hydrogen isn't a fuel problem, it's a where-do-you-use-it problem. So where would you use it: trucks, ships, steel, or storing power for a windless week? Tell me in the comments.
If you like seeing the hidden machinery behind everyday life, subscribe to Other End of the Wire. Every source behind the numbers in this video is in the description. Follow the electron.

meta.description:
Turn electricity into hydrogen and back, and a national lab test got only 28 to 35 percent of it back. A grid battery returns about 82.
So where does hydrogen actually make sense? We follow the electron from the outlet to the electrolyzer, the fuel tank, the fertilizer field and the steel mill.

In this video:
- Why hydrogen is an energy carrier, not an energy source
- How the U.S. makes about 10 million metric tons a year, mostly from natural gas
- Grey, blue and green hydrogen, and why DOE skips the colors
- Electrolysis losses and the round-trip problem vs. batteries
- Why hydrogen struggles in cars and home heating
- Where the molecule matters: refineries, ammonia/fertilizer, steel
- The maybes: shipping fuels, heavy trucks, long-duration storage
- The U.S. hydrogen hubs and national strategy
